full: The fulcrum the board built toward has resolved, and it broke dovish. June CPI, released 8:30am ET Tuesday 14-Jul, undershot across the board: headline fell 0.4% m/m — the biggest monthly decline in over six years, driven by a 5.7% drop in energy — taking the annual rate to 3.5% from May's 4.2% (consensus ~3.8%), while core was FLAT on the month (0.0%, the softest since January 2021) for a 2.6% annual rate versus a ~2.9% consensus. Markets read it as a green light to fade the imminent-hike fear: CME odds of a July hike collapsed from ~42% Monday to ~17%, the 2-year yield fell as much as ~14bp to ~4.14% (its biggest one-day drop since February) and the 10-year eased to ~4.58%, a clean bull-steepening. But two caveats keep it from being an all-clear: a September hike is still ~60% priced, and this is JUNE data — the July Brent spike to ~$86 is not in it. Fed Chair Warsh, in his first congressional testimony, leaned into exactly that, calling the print 'encouraging' but warning against anyone concluding 'mission accomplished', declining forward guidance and noting the Fed has now held four meetings running.

The banks turned the same 8:30am moment into a blow-out. JPMorgan posted net income of $21.2bn and EPS of $7.70 (~$6.14 ex-items) versus a ~$5.55 consensus, on revenue of ~$58bn (+27% YoY) with every business at a record and equities-trading revenue up 86% to ~$6.0bn — a 41% profit jump. Goldman Sachs delivered the best quarter in its history: EPS $20.98 against $10.91 a year earlier on ~$20.3bn of net revenue. Wells Fargo cleared estimates with net income of $6.4bn, EPS $2.00 and record revenue of ~$22.6bn. The engine was the same one that has stressed everyone else: Iran-war cross-asset volatility drove a trading frenzy, while investment banking rode a fee wave punctuated by last month's giant SpaceX IPO (~$500m in fees, Goldman and Morgan Stanley leading). The desk's pre-position on the banks printed in full — so banks-q2 flips to a post-print reaction, and the durable read-through is that the money-center market-makers are the cleanest listed way to be long geopolitical volatility.

The tape's other story was a single-name earthquake with a constructive read-through. IBM cratered 25% — its worst day on record, exceeding even October 1987 — after preannouncing a Q2 miss: adjusted EPS $2.93 versus $3.02 expected on revenue of $17.2bn (~3.7% light), erasing ~$68.8bn of value. CEO Arvind Krishna's explanation matters more than the miss: 'we faltered' on deals that slipped, and a late-June client capex rotation AWAY from software and mainframes and INTO supply-constrained AI servers, storage and memory. That is bearish for Big Blue but a direct, sourced tailwind for the memory and AI-hardware complex — and the tape agreed, with US semis rebounding (SMH +2.5%) even as IBM dragged the Dow to a flat close. The S&P 500 rose 0.38% to 7,543.59 and the Nasdaq gained 0.9% to 26,107 on the CPI relief and the chip bounce; the VIX fell to 16.5. It reinforces the AI-capex-is-real reversal the board already trades (mu-fq3-react, msft, tsm), not the capex-ceiling fear.

Asia took Wall Street's relief and ran with it, and the memory read-through was the overnight tell. Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed ~0.9% to above 68,300 and the Topix ~1% to ~4,080 (15-Jul), tracking the US higher as the softer CPI cut near-term hike bets — led by AI and memory names: Kioxia +6.7%, Lasertec +6.9%, Taiyo Yuden +5.7%, Advantest +4.4%, Tokyo Electron +1.6%. Investors looked past Trump's threat of additional strikes on Iran and the reinstated Hormuz blockade. The regional read is risk-on and semis-led, the mirror image of the memory panic that gripped Korea a week ago. Europe had already set the tone: on 14-Jul the FTSE 100 led the continent up 0.30% to 10,529.39, the DAX added ~0.1% and the CAC was roughly flat, early Iran risk-aversion giving way to relief on the US inflation print.

Rates, the dollar and gold all swung to the dovish read — and that is the board's re-tuned throughline. The front end rallied hardest (2Y ~4.14%) while the 10Y eased to ~4.58% and the 30Y held near ~5.06%, so quality carry is marginally richer but a boxed-in 10-year still sits mid-band under its proven 5% ceiling. The dollar cracked: DXY fell ~0.5% to ~100.7 (intraday low ~100.60), lifting EUR/USD ~0.6% to ~1.145 and cable ~0.5% to ~1.34 — both still short of the 1.17 / 1.355 triggers that would arm the tactical FX upside trades, so those stay held back, but the post-peak-dollar turn the hedge is sized for is visibly starting. Gold answered the CPI where it had refused the war, reversing its ~3% war-week slide to jump back toward $4,100 as the softer Fed outlook revived the bid — accumulate the structural/official-sector case, now with a friendlier near-term rate and dollar backdrop. USD/JPY sits ~162.2 near a 40-year low, the yen undercut by Japan's oil-import reliance even on a softer dollar, so the intervention binary into the 31-Jul BoJ stays genuinely two-sided — the long-vol strangle, not a directional bet, remains the honest expression.

exEarnings.thesis: The convexity trade the desk built has gone vertical and is now paying. A fortnight ago the STRUCTURAL picture was soft: Rory Johnston (Commodity Context) had read Hormuz flows recovering against weak Chinese demand, prompt contango re-emerging for the first time since February — a 'dour', mini-glut tape near $72 Brent. His W28 note (10-Jul) marks the turn: crude posted its largest weekly gain since mid-May as Iran's attempt to control Hormuz flows sparked skirmishes threatening the MOU-ceasefire collapse, and the curve snapped back from deepening contango toward prompt backwardation — the most violent week in Hormuz since the MOU. Then the escalation ran: on Monday President Trump ordered a naval blockade on Iranian ships/customers and Brent settled +9.59% at $83.30, its biggest daily gain since May 2020; on Tuesday Iran hit two UAE supertankers with cruise missiles — the crude carrier Mombasa (1 killed, 8 injured) and the LNG carrier Bahiya — and struck the US 5th Fleet's Bahrain base, taking Brent to ~$85.92 (+10% on the week); with Trump now demanding a 20% cargo levy on Hormuz transits and traffic down >50% (57 vessels Fri-Sun), the ~$80/$92 call spread is now in the money. The durability point holds and hardened — TSCS ('Nobody Has Seen The Supreme Leader', 8-Jul) reads the ceasefire's collapse as structural, the financial incentives that held it dismantled — and the struck LNG carrier extends the tail from crude into gas (Hormuz carries ~35% of global LPG, ~7% of LNG). A call spread bought when vol was cheap has worked into the escalation with premium defined. Bank gains into the spike and stay long the two-sided disruption tail via the call spread; if de-escalation returns the residual loss is capped and the structural glut re-takes over.
